Try each question before opening its answer. The probabilities are toy values chosen to test transfer, not experimental measurements.

## Check your understanding

### 1. Calculate centering for new values

A trainer's binary policy has $p_\theta(v=1)=p=0.4$. The sampler uses $q(v=1)=r=0.7$. The trainer scores are $s_1=1-p$ and $s_0=-p$.

Calculate the expected score under the sampler, then the two centered scores. Verify that their expectation under $q$ is zero.

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

The scores are $s_1=0.6$ and $s_0=-0.4$. Their expectation under the sampler is

$$
\bar{s}_q=rs_1+(1-r)s_0=0.7\times0.6+0.3\times(-0.4)=0.3=r-p.
$$

The centered scores are $\widetilde{s}_1=0.6-0.3=0.3$ and $\widetilde{s}_0=-0.4-0.3=-0.7$. Their expectation is

$$
0.7\times0.3+0.3\times(-0.7)=0.
$$

</details>

### 2. Recover the on-policy case

Keep $p=0.4$, but now assume the sampler uses $r=0.4$. What happens to $\bar{s}_q$? Why is the correction inactive?

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

When $q=p_\theta$, $\bar{s}_q=r-p=0$. The scores already have zero expectation under the distribution that samples them, so subtracting that expectation does not change them.

</details>

### 3. Distinguish three kinds of “centering”

Match each operation to its mathematical object:

- score centering;
- reward or advantage centering in GRPO;
- attention-score processing.

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

- **Score centering** subtracts, at each prefix, the sampler expectation of the gradient $\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(v\mid h)$.
- **Group centering** subtracts a group statistic from the rewards or advantages of rollouts for the same prompt.
- **Attention-score processing** acts on compatibility scores $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$ before softmax.

These objects have different dimensions and roles; sharing a word does not make them interchangeable.

</details>

### 4. Interpret the stat=ratio / stat=tv boundary

The implementation documents composition of score centering with corrections using stat=ratio and explicitly rejects stat=tv. Can we conclude that every correction based on total variation distance is mathematically invalid?

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. We can conclude that **this implementation** does not support this composition with stat=tv, and that the documented result covers compatible ratio-based corrections. A rejection in code is not a general proof of mathematical impossibility. Keep the scope of the theoretical result, the implementation contract, and methods that have not been studied separate.

</details>
